title: JGB Yield Curve Projections: What the Data Tells Us
abstract: A careful look at the signals from Japan's bond market, and why the curve's shape may matter more than the level.
body:
## Introduction

I spent a decade inside a central bank, and the habit that stuck hardest is the one I find least welcome at dinner parties: I insist on separating what a central bank said from what the market did. They are different objects, measured differently, and they answer different questions. This newsletter is an attempt to apply that habit to the Japanese government bond curve, which has been the most interesting object in fixed income for some time now. I write this on 2026-10-05, with the usual caveat that anything I say about the Bank of Japan is my reading of public communication, not a leak, and anything I say about the market is a reading of prices, not a forecast.

Let me start with why the curve, rather than the ten-year yield, deserves the attention. The ten-year yield is a single number that compresses an enormous amount of information. The curve, by contrast, tells you what different maturities are pricing about policy, term premium, and supply. When a central bank is changing its framework, the curve is where the disagreement shows up first. The level can be anchored by a policy rate that everyone knows. The shape is where the argument lives.

## What the Bank Said

The Bank of Japan has, over the past several years, moved from yield curve control to something that looks more like a flexible framework with occasional bond purchases. The communication has been careful, and I want to be equally careful in describing it. The bank has said that it will conduct bond purchases in a manner that keeps long-term rates from rising too rapidly, while allowing the curve to form more naturally. It has also said that it does not target a specific level for the ten-year yield. Those two statements are not contradictory, but they leave a lot of room for interpretation, and markets have interpreted them.

What the bank has not said, at least not in plain language, is what it considers an acceptable slope. This is the gap that makes the curve so interesting. A central bank that does not specify a slope has effectively delegated the term premium to the market, while retaining the option to intervene if the market's answer is too aggressive. That is a framework, but it is a framework with a wide tolerance band, and wide tolerance bands are where volatility lives.

I should also note the fiscal side, because it is not separable. The government's issuance calendar matters for the long end, and the bank's purchases matter for the same maturities. When both are changing, the curve is being pulled by two hands, and it is not always obvious which hand is stronger. I do not have a strong view on which dominates, and I am suspicious of anyone who claims to.

## What the Market Did

Now the market. Over the past year, the Japanese curve has steepened, with the long end rising more than the short end. That is a factual statement about prices, and I want to keep it at that level. The interpretation is where it gets contested. One reading is that the market is pricing a normalization of term premium after years of suppression. Another is that the market is pricing fiscal risk. A third is that the market is simply following global long rates, which have also moved. These are not mutually exclusive, and I would not want to assign weights without more evidence.

What I can say is that the steepening has been orderly, in the sense that it has not been accompanied by the kind of dysfunction that would force the bank to intervene aggressively. The bank has conducted operations, and the operations have been absorbed. That is a signal, but a weak one. It tells you that the market can handle the current pace, not that it can handle a faster one.

I also want to flag the role of foreign investors. They have been marginal buyers and sellers at different points, and their behavior is sensitive to hedging costs, which are sensitive to rate differentials. When the differential moves, the flow moves, and the curve feels it. This is not a Japanese story alone. It is a global story with a Japanese chapter.

## The Projection Question

People ask me for projections, and I try to give them a framework instead. A projection of the curve is really three projections: a projection of the policy path, a projection of the term premium, and a projection of supply. The first is the bank's, the second is the market's, and the third is the government's. When you put them together, you get a curve, but you also get a lot of error bars.

My own framework is simple. I start with the policy path implied by overnight index swaps, which is a market measure, not a forecast. I then ask what term premium would be consistent with that path and with current supply. If the actual curve is steeper than that, the market is either pricing more policy tightening than the swaps suggest, or pricing more term premium, or both. I do not resolve the ambiguity. I just note it.

What I would watch, if I were still inside the bank, is the relationship between the ten-year and the thirty-year. That spread is where the term premium argument is most visible. If it widens without a change in the policy path, the market is telling you something about duration supply or about inflation risk. If it narrows while the policy path is unchanged, the market is telling you something about demand for duration. Either way, it is information.

## Conclusion

I will end where I began, with the distinction between what was said and what was done. The Bank of Japan has said it will allow the curve to form more naturally. The market has allowed it to steepen. Those two facts are consistent, but they do not tell us where the curve goes next. For that, we need to watch the policy path, the term premium, and the supply calendar, and we need to be honest about how little we know about each. I will keep writing about this as the data comes in, and I will keep hedging, because that is what the data deserves.
